title: Force Track: Push, Roll, Pull
intro: Push a box, track a rolling ball, and test a magnet that never touches anything. Change one thing, predict, release.
note: This is a model that uses the lesson's backup dot table. The real ramp, rolling-ball, and magnet tests in the lesson still count. Keep real magnets away from Chromebooks. Use only large ceramic or ferrite magnets and keep every magnet out of mouths.
summary: Equal pushes canceled and the box stayed still; unequal pushes moved it the way the bigger push points. The model ball kept even gaps (0, 10, 20, 30 cm gave 40 cm; 0, 8, 16, 24 cm gave 32 cm), so the next dot could be predicted from the pattern. The magnet pulled iron and steel without touching, but not the penny or foil. Magnets do not pull all metals.

reads.q: When are the forces on an object balanced?

choices.label: When equal forces cancel, so motion does not change
choices.why: Yes. Equal pushes canceled and the box stayed still.

choices.label: Whenever two forces act at the same time
choices.why: Two forces acted in every test, but the box moved twice. They balance only when they are equal.

choices.label: Only when nothing is pushing at all
choices.why: The box was pushed from both sides and still did not move. Equal forces balanced.

rounds.finding: Equal pushes balanced and the box stayed still. Unequal pushes moved it the way the bigger push points.

rounds.question: A model ball rolls with no friction. Its position is marked every second. Where is the next dot?

predict.q: Where is the dot at 4 seconds?

options.label: Run the model ball
options.hint: look at the gaps between the dots so far. What do you notice about them?

reads.q: The gaps between dots stay the same. What does that say about the forces?

choices.label: They are nearly balanced, so the motion hardly changes
choices.why: Yes. Even gaps mean even motion, which matches balanced forces.

choices.label: A force must be keeping it going
choices.why: No force is needed to keep it going. Balanced forces keep motion the same.

choices.label: Friction is speeding it up
choices.why: Friction pushes against motion. It would make the gaps shrink, not stay even.

reads.q: A real ball rolled on carpet slows down. What would its dots do?

choices.label: Get closer together
choices.why: Yes. Friction is an unbalanced force against the motion, so the ball covers less ground each second.

choices.label: Get farther apart
choices.why: That would mean speeding up. Nothing pushes the ball faster on carpet.

choices.label: Stay exactly even, like the model
choices.why: The model has no friction. A real ball on carpet has friction, and friction slows it.

rounds.finding: The model ball's dots kept even gaps: 0, 10, 20, 30 cm, so 4 seconds lands at 40 cm. A motion pattern lets us predict.

alt.question: A new run of the model ball. Same rule: no friction, a mark every second. Where is the next dot?

options.label: Run the model ball
options.hint: look at the gap between each pair of dots, then count on from 24.

alt.finding: The second run kept even gaps too: 0, 8, 16, 24 cm, so 4 seconds lands at 32 cm.

rounds.question: The magnet never touches anything. Which objects does it pull?
rounds.change: The object held near the magnet

predict.q: Pulled by the magnet, or not?

options.label: Penny
options.hint: check what a penny is made of. Does a magnet pull everything made of metal?

options.label: Aluminum foil
options.hint: check what foil is made of. Does a magnet pull everything made of metal?

options.label: Eraser
options.hint: what is an eraser made of?

choices.label: Magnets pull iron and some steels, not every metal
choices.why: Yes. The iron pieces moved; the other metals did not.

choices.label: Magnets pull all metals
choices.why: Some metals in your test did not move. All-metal is the wrong rule.

choices.label: Magnets pull everything small
choices.why: Material matters, not size. Look at which small things stayed.

reads.q: The clip moved, but the magnet never touched it. What does that show?

choices.label: Some pushes and pulls act without touching
choices.why: Yes. Magnetic force reaches across a small gap.

choices.label: The table must have shaken
choices.why: The other objects sat on the same table and did not move. The magnet caused it.

choices.label: The clip started moving on its own
choices.why: Objects do not start moving on their own. An unbalanced force from the magnet moved it.

rounds.finding: The magnet pulled the iron nail and the steel clip without touching them. The penny, foil, and eraser did not move: magnets do not pull all metals.

options.label: Aluminum can
options.hint: aluminum is a metal, but not every metal sticks.

options.label: Penny
options.hint: a penny is copper and zinc.

alt.finding: The magnet pulled the iron bolt and the iron nail without touching them. The can, button, and penny did not move.

choices.label: keep motion the same; unbalanced forces change it.
choices.why: The box stayed when pushes were equal and moved when they were not.

choices.label: are needed to keep an object moving.
choices.why: The model ball kept even gaps with nothing pushing it. Balanced forces do not change motion, whether the object is still or moving.

choices.label: let us predict the next dot: the gaps stay the same, so the next dot is one more gap along.
choices.why: Even gaps, same step, next point predicted.

choices.label: can never tell us what happens next.
choices.why: You just predicted the next dot from the pattern.

choices.label: can pull iron or steel without touching, but not all metals.
choices.why: That is exactly what the pull test showed.

choices.label: pulls every kind of metal.
choices.why: Some metals in the test did not move.
